processing: A factory blend of raw large-leaf mao cha, steamed and pressed into a cake, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Blended from stock, so no single picking applies; what matters is the production year and batch.
appearance_dry: A 357 g cake of coarser, larger leaf than the factory's finer recipes, dark green to brown with age.
appearance_liquor: Golden in young cakes, turning amber to reddish with age.
appearance_wet: Larger, sturdy leaf with some stem, olive when young and darker with age.
taste_profile: Few reliable notes are specific to this recipe. As with other classic Menghai raw blends, expect strength and bitterness when young, with woodier, deeper tones after long storage.

brewing.notes: Rinse aged cakes once; brew young ones short and gently.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and batch, usually as a 357 g cake. Recipe numbers are not made every year in the same way, and the collectable market focuses on older releases, whose wrappers are often faked. Ask for the year and batch number and how it was stored.
description:
7582 is one of the numbered raw recipes of the Menghai Tea Factory. It belongs to the same family of export codes as 7542 and 7532, which is why collectors speak of it as a 'classic recipe' and not a place.

By the usual reading of these codes, the last digit 2 stands for Menghai and the third digit 8 for a main leaf grade around grade 8, on the coarser side. The first two digits are often read as a recipe year, though that reading is not firmly settled for this code.

It is a cake to drink for its factory style. As with other Menghai raw blends it is strong when young and asks for time. Reliable recipe-specific tasting notes are scarce, so try one before you buy a stack.

For older cakes, storage and provenance matter more than the number on the wrapper. Fakes of well-known Dayi years exist, so buy from sellers who can show the batch.
history: In 1979 Menghai Tea Factory's export pressed teas began to diversify beyond 7452 and 7572, and 7542, 7532 and 7582 are recorded as the new blend codes of that time. Accounts of its later production disagree, including on when it was first made and how steadily it stayed in the range. The factory's Dayi brand came later and became its main label from the late 1980s and 1990s.
